{{Short description|Florentine mathematician and astronomer (1282–1374)}}
[[File:Abbaco manuscript.jpg|thumb|Text from a manuscript of his ''Trattato d'Abbaco'' in Paolo's own handwriting]]
'''Paolo Dagomari da Prato''' (1282&ndash;1374), known in [[Latin language|Latin]] as '''Paulus Geometrus''' (''Paolo il Geometra'', "Paul the Geometer"), was a noted [[Republic of Florence|Florentine]] [[mathematician]] and [[astronomer]], such a ''maestro dell'abbaco'' (master/teacher of the [[abacus]]) that he gained the epithet '''Paolo dell'Abbaco'''. [[Franco Sacchetti]] called him ''Paolo Arismetra e Astrologo'' (arithmetician and astronomer) and [[Giorgio Vasari]] ''Paulo Strolago'' or ''Paolo Astrologo'' (astronomer). He reputedly had 6,000&ndash;10,000 pupils over the course of his life, being praised by contemporaries like [[Giovanni Gherardi da Prato]],<ref>''Il Dagomari a moltissimi, anzi a infiniti nella nostra Firenze fu in aritmetica diligentissimo maestro, rinovellatore di buone e utilissime regole, e principiò a scorgere la nostra città alle utili e leggiadre regole dell'algoritmo inaudito e morto per moltissimi secoli'' (''Paradiso degli Alberti'', Vol. II, p. 99)</ref> [[Filippo Villani]],<ref>''Questi fu geometra grandissimo, e peritissimo aritmetico e però nelle adequazioni astronomiche tutti gli antichi e moderni passò. Questi fu diligentissimo osservatore delle stelle e del movimento de'cieli, e dimostrò che al moderno tempo le tavole toletane erano o di poca o di niuna utilità e quelle d'Alfonso in alcuna varietà sensibile essere varie; donde dimostrò che Io strumento dell'astrolabio, misurato secondo la tavole toletane, il quale noi usiamo frequentemente, devia dalle regole d'astrologia: e quelli astronomi che di quindi pigliavano argomento dell'arte essere ingannati. Costui di tutti quelli del tempo nostro fu il primo che compose un Taccuino e di futuri avvenimenti compose molti annali'' (''Le vite d'uomini illustri fiorentini'', ed. Giammaria Mazzuchelli, Florence, 1847, p. 45).</ref> and [[Giovanni Villani]] in his ''Cronica''.<ref>''Nell'anno 1345, di'28 di Marzo, poco dopo l'ora di nona, secondo l'adequazione di mastro Pagolo, figliuolo di ser Piero, grande maestro in questa scienza d'astrologia, fu la congiunzione di Saturno e di Giove a gradi venti del segno dell' Aquario coll'infrascritto aspetto degli altri pianeti'' (''Cronica di Giovanni Villani a miglior lezione ridotta coll'aiuto de'testi a penna'', Vol. VII, book XII, chapt. XLI, p. 105).</ref>

Paolo was born at [[Prato]], the son of Piero Dagomari, who had moved to Florence. At Florence Paolo became the private tutor of [[Jacopo Alighieri]] and a friend of [[Giovanni Boccaccio]], who praised him highly in his ''[[De genealogia deorum gentilium]]''. The need for mathematics among the bankers and merchants of Florence led him to found a school of arithmetic (''[[Abacus school|bottegha d'abacho]]'') at [[Santa Trinita]].<ref>Markus A. Denzel, ''Kaufmannsbücher und Handelspraktiken vom Spätmittelalter bis zum beginnenden'' (Franz Steiner Verlag, 2002), p. 59</ref> In 1363 he held the [[priorate]] of the quarter of S. Spirito from May&ndash;June. Paolo died in Florence and was buried in Santa Trinita under a now-lost epitaph. His portrait, in [[fresco]], is painted on the vault of the [[Galleria degli Uffizi]].

In mathematics Paolo introduced the [[Period (punctuation)|period]] or [[Comma (punctuation)|comma]] as a device for separating numbers into groups of three for easing calculations on the order of thousands and millions. He is most famous for his work on [[equation]]s (''aequationibus'') that fused [[geometry]] and [[arithmetic]], which we today would recognise as [[algebra]]. His most important mathematical treatise was the ''Regoluzze'', a manual of elementary arithmetic, written in 1340. Some of the "little rules" are:<ref>Robert Sabatino Lopez and Irving W. Raymond, ''Medieval Trade in the Mediterranean World'' (New York: Columbia University Press, 1951), p. 341 n2.</ref>
<blockquote>
1. If you wish to write down [a number of] many figures, make a period at every third figure beginning from the right hand and going towards the left, and then you will have as many thousands as are in front of the periods.<br>
2. If you wish to multiply numbers ending with a zero, multiply their figures and put all of the zeros at the end.<br>
15. If you wish to multiply fraction by fraction, multiply the numerators with one another, and the denominators similarly.<br>
32. If you multiply the width of a circle by 22 and divide by 7,  you will have the circumference.
</blockquote>
